name: Brisk Walking
summary: Walking fast enough to raise your breathing while still being able to hold a conversation. The most accessible cardio there is, and it counts toward your weekly activity target.
steps: Wear comfortable, supportive shoes and start with five minutes at an easy pace to warm up.
Speed up until your breathing is clearly faster but you can still talk in full sentences. If you could sing, go faster.
Walk tall with your eyes on the horizon, shoulders relaxed and elbows bent, swinging your arms forward and back.
Land softly on your heel and roll through to push off your toes. To go faster, take quicker steps, not much longer ones.
Hold that pace for 10 to 30 minutes, depending on your fitness, and build up gradually over the weeks.
Finish with a few minutes of easy walking to bring your breathing back down.
cues: Walk as if you are slightly late
mistakes: Strolling too gently to raise your breathing rate
Overstriding, which puts the brakes on every step
Looking down at a phone and hunching forward
Doing too much too soon after a long break
easier: Break it into three 10-minute walks spread through the day.
harder: Add hills, short faster intervals or a light backpack, or extend the walk toward 45 to 60 minutes.

name: Running
summary: Vigorous, time-efficient cardio that needs only shoes and a route. It builds heart and lung fitness well, provided you increase how much you run gradually.
steps: Warm up with five to ten minutes of brisk walking or very easy jogging.
Run at an easy effort at which you can speak in short sentences. Most of your running should feel this comfortable.
Run tall with a slight forward lean from the ankles, eyes ahead, shoulders loose and elbows bent to about 90 degrees.
Take quick, light steps so your feet land under your body, not far out in front of it.
If you are new to running, alternate one minute of running with two minutes of walking for 20 to 30 minutes, and lengthen the running portions week by week.
Cool down with five minutes of walking. At first, leave at least a day between runs so muscles, tendons and bones can adapt.
cues: Run tall, lean slightly from the ankles
mistakes: Starting too fast and having to stop after a few minutes
Increasing distance or frequency too quickly
Overstriding, with a heavy heel strike far ahead of the body
Running hard in every session, with no easy days
Pushing on through sharp or worsening pain
easier: Use run-walk intervals, or build a base with brisk walking first.
harder: Extend one run each week, or add short faster efforts such as six rounds of one minute quick, two minutes easy.

name: Cycling
summary: Pedaling outdoors or on a stationary bike gives you a solid cardio workout with very little impact on your joints. Easy to adjust, from a gentle spin to an all-out effort.
steps: Set the saddle height so your knee keeps a slight bend at the bottom of the pedal stroke and your hips do not rock from side to side.
Start with five minutes of easy pedaling in a light gear or at low resistance.
Settle into a steady effort at which your breathing is deeper but you can still talk, pedaling at a smooth rhythm of about 60 to 90 turns per minute.
Keep your shoulders relaxed, elbows slightly bent and knees tracking straight over the pedals.
Ride for 20 to 45 minutes. For a harder session, add intervals such as one minute hard followed by two minutes easy, repeated six to eight times.
Finish with five minutes of easy spinning. Outdoors, wear a helmet and follow local road rules.
cues: Spin a lighter gear, do not grind
mistakes: A saddle set too low, which loads the front of the knees
A saddle set too high, which makes the hips rock
Grinding a heavy gear at a very slow cadence
Locking the elbows and hunching the shoulders
easier: Lower the resistance and ride for 10 to 15 minutes, adding a few minutes each week.
harder: Add hills or resistance, lengthen the ride, or include hard intervals.

name: Rowing Machine
summary: A full-body cardio machine that works legs, trunk and back together with no impact. The stroke takes a little learning, and good technique makes it far more effective.
steps: Strap your feet in across the widest part of each foot and set the resistance low to moderate. Hold the handle with relaxed hands.
Start at the front of the stroke: shins vertical, arms straight, shoulders just in front of your hips and back flat.
Drive by pushing with your legs first. As your legs straighten, swing your torso back slightly, then pull the handle to your lower ribs.
Recover in the reverse order: arms out, torso forward from the hips, then bend your knees and slide forward.
Make the drive powerful and the recovery about twice as long. For steady rowing, that works out to roughly 20 to 26 strokes per minute.
Row easily for five minutes, then hold a steady effort for 10 to 20 minutes or alternate hard and easy minutes. Finish with a few easy minutes.
cues: Legs, body, arms. Then arms, body, legs
Push with the legs before you pull
Flat back, hinge from the hips
mistakes: Pulling with the arms before the legs have pushed
Rounding the lower back at the front of the stroke
Setting the resistance to maximum and grinding
Rushing up the slide, so the stroke becomes choppy
Leaning far back at the finish
easier: Row for one to two minutes at a time with short rests, focusing on the order of the stroke.
harder: Extend the steady rowing, or do intervals such as eight rounds of one minute hard and one minute easy.

name: Swimming
summary: Full-body cardio with the water supporting your weight, which makes it gentle on joints. It trains heart, lungs and upper body together, at whatever pace you choose.
steps: Choose a lane that matches your speed and warm up with two to four easy lengths in any stroke.
For front crawl, keep your body long and level with your eyes on the pool floor, and kick gently and steadily from the hips.
Reach forward with each arm, then pull back under your body and past your hip. Let your body rotate slightly with each stroke.
Breathe out steadily while your face is in the water, and turn your head to the side to breathe in. Do not lift it forward.
Swim lengths at an effort that keeps your breathing under control, resting 15 to 30 seconds at the wall as needed, for 15 to 30 minutes in total.
Finish with a couple of easy lengths. Swim where a lifeguard is on duty, and never alone in open water.
cues: Reach, then pull past the hip
mistakes: Holding your breath underwater and gasping each time you turn your head
Lifting the head forward to breathe, which sinks the legs
Kicking from the knees with big splashes
Sprinting the first lengths and fading fast
easier: Rest at each wall, use a kickboard or switch to a gentler stroke. If you cannot swim yet, start with adult lessons.
harder: Shorten the rests, swim longer continuous sets, or add faster lengths between easy ones.

name: Jump Rope
summary: Skipping rope packs a lot of cardio into a small space and a short time, and it sharpens footwork and coordination. The impact is real, so build up in short rounds.
steps: Size the rope: stand on its middle with one foot and check that the handles reach about armpit height. Jump on a firm surface with a little give, such as a wooden floor or a mat.
Hold the handles with your elbows close to your sides and your hands just in front of your hips.
Turn the rope with small circles of your wrists, not big swings of your arms.
Jump just high enough to clear the rope, about 2 to 3 cm (1 inch), and land softly on the balls of your feet with knees slightly bent.
Start with rounds of 20 to 30 seconds followed by equal rest, for five to ten minutes in total.
Lengthen the rounds gradually as your calves and coordination adapt, and finish with an easy walk.
mistakes: Jumping far higher than the rope requires
Swinging the whole arm from the shoulder
Landing flat-footed or on stiff legs
Doing long sessions before your calves and Achilles tendons are ready
easier: Practice the jump rhythm without a rope, or step over the rope one foot at a time.
harder: Extend rounds to one to three minutes, or try alternate-foot steps and faster turns.

name: Stair Climbing
summary: Climbing stairs lifts your whole body weight with every step, so it raises your heart rate fast and strengthens your legs. Any staircase will do.
steps: Find a safe staircase with a handrail, or use a stair-climbing machine. Walk on the flat or climb slowly for three to five minutes to warm up.
Climb at a steady pace, placing your whole foot on each step and pushing up through the heel and midfoot.
Stand tall with a slight forward lean from the hips, eyes on the steps ahead, and keep a hand near the rail.
On real stairs, walk back down slowly as your recovery, taking care with every step.
Repeat the climbs for 10 to 20 minutes in total, at an effort that makes full sentences difficult by the top.
Finish with a few minutes of easy walking on the flat.
cues: Tall chest, hand near the rail
mistakes: Hauling yourself up with the handrail, or leaning on the machine's console
Climbing on your toes only, which overloads the calves
Hurrying on the way down when your legs are tired
Hunching forward and staring at your feet
easier: Climb one flight at a time with a rest at the top, and use the rail for balance.
harder: Climb faster, take the stairs two at a time on the way up, or wear a light backpack.

name: Burpee
summary: A squat, a plank, a push-up and a jump stitched into one move. It drives your heart rate up fast with no equipment, as long as you keep the form tidy.
steps: Stand with your feet shoulder-width apart.
Squat down and place your hands on the floor just in front of your feet.
Step or jump your feet back into a high plank, abs tight so your hips do not sag.
Lower your chest to the floor with a push-up, then press back up to the plank.
Step or jump your feet forward to land outside your hands with your heels down.
Stand up and finish with a small jump, reaching your arms overhead. Land softly with bent knees and go straight into the next rep.
Work in short sets, such as 5 to 10 reps or 20 to 30 seconds, resting long enough to keep every rep clean.
cues: Hips stay level in the plank
Feet land flat before you stand
A steady pace beats a sloppy sprint
mistakes: Letting the hips sag as the feet jump back
Landing on the toes with the knees caving in
Rounding the back and standing up with straight legs
Racing until the form falls apart
easier: Step your feet back and forward instead of jumping, and skip the push-up and the jump at the top.
harder: Add a tuck jump at the top, or do timed rounds such as 30 seconds of work and 30 seconds of rest.

name: Jumping Jack
summary: The schoolyard classic: jumping your feet out while your arms swing overhead. A quick, equipment-free way to warm up or raise your heart rate in a small space.
steps: Stand tall with your feet together and your arms at your sides.
Jump your feet out to a little wider than shoulder-width while swinging your arms out and up until your hands meet, or nearly meet, overhead.
Land softly on the balls of your feet with knees slightly bent and pointing the same way as your toes.
Jump straight back to the start, feet together and arms at your sides.
Keep a steady rhythm for 20 to 60 seconds, rest, and repeat for three to five rounds. As a warm-up, one or two minutes is plenty.
cues: Find a rhythm you can hold
mistakes: Landing heavily on stiff legs
Letting the knees collapse inward on landing
Half-hearted arm swings that stop at shoulder height
Arching the lower back as the arms go overhead
easier: Step one foot out to the side at a time while raising your arms, with no jump.
harder: Go faster, add a squat each time your feet land wide, or extend the rounds.

name: Incline Treadmill Walk
summary: Walking uphill on a treadmill raises your heart rate far more than walking on the flat, without the impact of running. A way to make walking properly hard that is gentle on the joints.
steps: Start with the treadmill flat and walk at a comfortable pace for three to five minutes.
Raise the incline in stages to between 5% and 10%, at a speed you can walk without holding on. For many people that is 4 to 6 km/h (2.5 to 3.7 mph).
Walk tall with a slight forward lean from the ankles, swinging your arms naturally.
Take slightly shorter steps than you would on the flat and push off through your whole foot.
Hold an effort at which you can speak in short sentences for 15 to 30 minutes, or alternate a few minutes steep with a few minutes flat.
Lower the incline and slow down for three to five minutes before stepping off.
cues: Tall posture, slight lean from the ankles
mistakes: Gripping the handrails and leaning back, which takes away most of the work
Setting the incline or speed too high to walk naturally
Hunching forward from the waist
Jumping straight to a steep grade without warming up the calves
easier: Use a 2% to 4% incline and a slower speed, building up over several weeks.
harder: Raise the incline toward 12% to 15%, lengthen the session, or add a light backpack.
